personas.persona: Sets the firm's writing culture and owns the decisions the narrative treats as unabsorbable: scope, conflicts, and when to decline a matter. She insists that anything a client reads carry full names and titles, and she signs client-facing documents formally even where colleagues use a shorter first name for her around the office. Her own prose is spare and deliberate; she edits certainty out of a memo and treats an unqualified sentence as a liability.

A prosecution partner who carries portfolio work and reviews it family by family, in long, structured passes. She writes freedom-to-operate memoranda that hedge every conclusion and mark themselves privileged, and would never let 'this does not infringe' stand without qualification. Formal and exacting in anything a client reads, she is faster and blunter with associates, quick to redline a claim chart that overreaches.

A prosecution associate still settling into the firm's house style, drafting responses and claim amendments under a partner's review. Careful and literal, she leans toward over-qualifying rather than overstating, which is exactly the reflex this firm rewards. Her client updates are short and pinned to a docket number, and she confirms a date twice before anything leaves her outbox.

A prosecution associate who handles the steady flow of office-action responses and portfolio upkeep. Organized and matter-of-fact, she writes to be understood by the docketing desk as much as by a client, keeping updates brief and anchored to the docket. She has absorbed the firm's allergy to overstatement and rarely commits to a conclusion she cannot footnote.

Keeper of the firm's religion, the docket. Nothing goes out and no deadline passes without routing through her, and she treats a missed date as the one mistake the practice cannot absorb. Her messages are terse, precise, and unsentimental, built from docket numbers and dates, with no patience for ambiguity about who owes what by when.

A prosecution associate comfortable deep in a specification and file history, working the technical side alongside the agents. He writes cleanly and conservatively, defers to a partner on anything a client will read, and marks privileged work as privileged without being told. His voice is plain and unshowy, the register of someone who would rather be correct than quotable.

A patent agent focused on drafting and prosecution before the office rather than client-facing counsel. He works deep in the technical detail and writes specifications and responses with an engineer's precision, leaving legal conclusions to the attorneys. His internal notes are dense and exact, and he flags anything touching infringement or validity up to a partner instead of opining himself.

A patent agent who prosecutes the firm's hardware-heavy matters and is fluent in the language of claims and drawings. Methodical and detail-obsessed, she keeps her work tightly scoped and hands anything resembling an opinion to counsel. Her writing is compact and neutral, built to survive a file wrapper rather than to persuade a reader.

A patent agent carrying a full prosecution docket, at home in office actions and examiner interviews. He is pragmatic and economical on the page, tracking every response against its docket number and never letting a deadline drift. He writes to the record rather than the reader, and routes the questions the firm treats as liabilities to the attorneys.

A patent agent grounded in the technical detail of the firm's device and hardware prosecution. Precise and understated, he drafts and amends claims with care and stays firmly inside the line between agent and attorney, escalating opinion work rather than venturing it. His prose is efficient and hedged by instinct, shaped by a practice that reads an unqualified statement as a risk.
